extracted.intended_audience: conference area chairs / meta-reviewers (ACL, EMNLP, similar NLP conferences), especially first-time ACs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Area Chair / meta-reviewer role for NLP conferences: responsibilities, time expectations, interaction with reviewers/SACs, and a template for writing meta-reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities of an Area Chair / Meta-Reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Look through the initial reviews (usually three), make a recommendation whether the paper is ready to be published, and write a short so-called meta-review summarizing the major points of the reviews as well as the reviewers’ discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be the safety net when initial reviews are unreliable: check reviews, discussion, and author response and synthesize them for SACs/PCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time commitment and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Area chairing is time-intensive; expect to spend significant time per paper (estimates given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates: ~10 minutes per paper to check reviewer assignment; at least ~30 minutes per paper to read reviews and start discussion; 45 minutes to 2+ hours per paper to read all material and write the meta-review. For many papers this sums to multiple full days. If you accept the role, block days in your calendar early. Conference organizers should allow more time (e.g., two weeks) for thorough meta-reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check reviewer assignment quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine reviewer assignment for potential problems before review discussion begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend about 10 minutes per paper early on to spot conflicts, expertise mismatches, or other assignment issues and raise them if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiate and moderate reviewer discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Read all reviews thoroughly and start a discussion among reviewers when further opinions or elaboration are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count on at least ~30 minutes per paper on average to read reviews and seed/coordinate discussion. Prompt reviewers, keep discussion productive, and follow up (e.g., say 'I haven't gotten to this yet but I will tomorrow' if delayed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do additional investigation when reviews are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If initial reviews appear unreliable or reviewers miss important points, dig deeper yourself (e.g., check prior work or read the paper more carefully).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may need to spend substantially more time on some cases (1–2+ hours) and occasionally write up points that look like mini-reviews to convince SAC/PCs of your view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: keep an initial/concise SUMMARY
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the meta-review with 2–3 sentences summarizing what the paper is about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise; do not repeat the paper's contribution list verbatim — give the AC's succinct view of the paper's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: STRENGTHS and CONTRIBUTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: State the reasons to accept the paper, noting the points you consider real contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply mirror the paper's own claims; highlight what you judge to be genuine contributions and why they matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: WEAKNESSES
rubrics_metrics.description: List things to be improved, especially for rejected papers (e.g., methodological flaws, missing comparisons with prior work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind the state of the literature at the submission deadline when judging missing comparisons. Be specific about the flaws or gaps that affect acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: WRITING and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on whether the writing is clear enough or needs improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between substantive scientific/technical problems and presentation issues; indicate whether clarity issues are minor and fixable for camera-ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: REVIEWS and DISCUSSION summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize what the reviewers recommend and what happened in the discussion, keeping double-blind constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include salient points from the author response where relevant, and clearly record where reviewers agree or disagree. Maintain anonymity and avoid revealing identities or de-anonymizing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: final SUMMARY / evaluation sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short summary of your overall evaluation of the paper (e.g., 'needs only minor modifications' or 'would profit from another iteration').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not state your explicit accept/reject recommendation in the text of the meta-review (because the PC decision may differ); instead give a clear evaluative summary that justifies your scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: ADDITIONAL COMMENTS when disagreeing with reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: When you disagree with initial reviews (or only agree with some reviewers), state the specific points that show you took a closer look and why you reached a different conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the reasons for disagreement; e.g., explain that a requested experiment is out of scope or that reviewers raised minor points irrelevant to acceptability. This is very helpful to SACs and PCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not state explicit recommendation in the meta-review text
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid explicitly stating 'accept' or 'reject' in the textual meta-review because higher-level decisions may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evaluative language and final-summary phrasing rather than a direct recommendation; scores submitted separately will communicate your recommendation to PCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive, polite, and useful (especially for rejected papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that behind many submissions are junior researchers; they deserve polite, useful feedback explaining why their paper was not accepted or what to improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide actionable comments and avoid dismissive language. Good meta-reviews can help authors improve and maintain a positive reviewing culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a clear stance when reviews are mixed
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs have more time than SACs and should not be afraid to weigh in and take sides when reviews give mixed signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which reviewer points you find decisive and why (e.g., 'one reviewer asked for X, but in my view this is beyond the scope of the paper'). Clear adjudication helps SACs/PCs triage borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain timely communication with SAC/PC and peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond promptly to coordination requests and keep SACs informed about progress or delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even brief status messages ('I will get to this tomorrow') are helpful when coordinating many ACs; lack of timely responses causes coordination burden.
